articles.summary: Perdieron ante los Clippers con un último tiro fallado por el MVP de la pasada temporada
articles.body: Los Thunder reaccionaron a las devastadoras bajas que tuvieron ganando varios partidos, lo que demostraba su enorme fondo de armario. Ante los Clippers, 113-112 sufrieron su tercera derrota consecutiva, lo que demuestra que esas bajas son aún más influyentes que su amplia plantilla. Va a ser una temporada complicada para uno de los equipos que salía como favorito al título en octubre. Ni una soberbia actuación de Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, que firmó 40 puntos, ni la segunda titularidad seguida juntos de Aday Mara e Isaiah Hartenstein, cuarta en lo que va de temporada, salvó a los Thunder de la derrota. Lo tuvieron cerca, pero una jugada magistral de Darius Garland a 50 segundos para el final, decantó el triunfo para los angelinos. En realidad, los Clippers, que perdían 106-112 a 2:43, empezaron a ganar antes, con un parcial de 7-0 que culminó Garland con su jugada. Fue una penetración en la que anotó una complicada canasta y sacó falta. El tiro libre ponía a los Clippers por delante a falta de 50.4 segundos. En la última posesión, Shai falló su tiro sobre la bocina y dejó la victoria en L.A., sumiendo a su equipo en una pequeña crisis de tres derrotas seguidas por primera vez en la temporada. Los Thunder son ahora octavos en el Oeste con 8-5. El partido, por cierto, pertenecía a la segunda jornada de la NBA Cup. Aday Mara, como queda dicho titular de nuevo, jugó 21 minutos aportando 10 puntos en 5/6 en tiros de campo con tres rebotes y tres tapones. En el cinco titular de Oklahoma, Jared McCain se fue hasta los 23 puntos con 7/11 en triples y Hartenstein hizo 21. Los titulares de OKC anotaron 102 de los 112 puntos del equipo. En los Clippers, Brook Lopez lideró a su equipo con 26 puntos, mientras que Garland le secundó con 24 y esa jugada de tres puntos final que fue decisiva. Baba Miller no dispuso de ningún minuto de juego en lo que fue la tercera victoria de la temporada de los angelinos.

articles.title: 1 Word To Describe Every NBA Team After 3 Weeks
articles.summary: Three weeks may not seem like much of a sample in an NBA season that'll eventually span six months, but it's more than enough to make some early assessments for all 30 teams.
articles.body:
Three weeks may not seem like much of a sample in an NBA season that'll eventually span six months, but it's more than enough to make some early assessments for all 30 teams.

To do that, we'll assign one word to encapsulate every squad's start, touching on major storylines, key stats and anything else that helps provide a sense of how things have gone so far.

Victor Wembanyama and the San Antonio Spurs are surging while still figuring things out. Luka Dončić is on a scoring blitz. The Oklahoma City Thunder have somehow held it together despite a rash of injuries to critically important players.

Let's check in on those teams and all the rest three weeks into the 2026-27 season.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LA Clippers | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

The Atlanta Hawks were having a hard time creating shots consistently with their starters because the otherwise talented group lacked on-ball zip. So veteran guard CJ McCollum solved the issue by going to head coach Quin Snyder and suggesting that rookie Kingston Flemings should take over his starting spot .

The quality of opposition has been a factor, but Atlanta went 3-1 across the first four Flemings' starts. In two wins against the Washington Wizards and one against the Brooklyn Nets, the Hawks put up three straight offensive ratings of at least 117.0—something they hadn't done at any previous point in the season.

It'd be irresponsible to say the change was owed entirely to Flemings, but he scored in double digits, got downhill and shot at least 55.6 percent from the field in all three wins. Meanwhile, McCollum stabilized the bench.

Maybe the Hawks' main issue is still their lack of a true superstar, but they'll outplay their talent if everyone continues to make ego-free decisions.

Swap in Paul George and Mitchell Robinson for Jaylen Brown, and the Boston Celtics' wildly successful operation continues to run like clockwork.

This week's marquee matchup with Brown's Philadelphia 76ers saw the Celtics continue to bomb threes, move the ball and defend with purpose—just like they've done for the last half-dozen years. The familiar result: an easy win.

Boston is once again among the league's top five in both offensive and defensive efficiency. As usual, the Celtics are among the NBA leaders in three-point frequency. Personnel changes, even seemingly seismic ones, don't seem to matter. Boston just continues to play its game, trust the math and blow away the competition.

Those who pilloried the Celtics for the Brown trade can still hope the former Finals MVP will be missed in the playoffs, when Boston's finely tuned system sometimes breaks down. For now, this team is wired tight and doing exactly what it always has, with Jayson Tatum atop the pecking order and head coach Joe Mazzulla at the controls.

The Brooklyn Nets still don't have a quality win (beating Charlotte, Indiana and New Orleans doesn't count). They're struggling mightily to put points on the board most nights, but at least they're kind of a pain to play against.

Brooklyn ranks among the league's top 10 in opponent turnover rate and has eight regulars in the rotation averaging at least 1.0 steal per 36 minutes. That number climbs to 10 if you include Egor Demin and Terance Mann, who've both missed time.

Second-year guard Nolan Traoré has become a regular starter. He leads all Nets who've played at least 100 minutes with a whopping 2.3 thefts per 36. Paired with his intriguing development as a scoring threat (61.1 effective field-goal percentage), he's emerged as a real bright spot next to prized rookie Mikel Brown Jr.

The Charlotte Hornets' season will be defined by what the team can and can't do without LaMelo Ball, a player whose critics often labeled him "unserious." So far, the Hornets are missing some of the wild, chaotic unpredictability their former point guard delivered.

Injuries to Kon Knueppel, Brandon Miller and Coby White foreseeably defanged Charlotte's attack in the early going, but the team's offense continued to underwhelm during a six-game losing streak from Oct. 28 to Nov. 6. Naz Reid has had his moments. This group will look punchier when everyone is ramped up to full speed, but something is undeniably missing from an offense that took the league by storm for most of last year.

It turns out the Hornets could use a little more unseriousness.

It'd be easy to cite the Chicago Bulls' No. 30 ranking in defensive efficiency, make fun of them by choosing "permissive" as their word and move on. But we've learned enough about early-season stats to know that there's almost always something random underlying a stat like this.

In Chicago's case, it's the typical culprit of red-hot opponent shooting.

Teams playing the Bulls are drilling a ridiculous 40.8 percent of their threes, the highest mark in the NBA so far.

While it's true Chicago's defensive personnel is wanting, particularly on the perimeter, that number is mostly out of the players' hands. Where the defense has more control, like near the rim, the Bulls are actually pretty solid. They rank among the top 10 in limiting opponents' conversion rates at the basket.

Pair that fact with the even bigger luck gap on the other end—the Bulls are second in location-based expected effective field-goal percentage but 28th in actual effective field-goal percentage—and you've got a whole lot of bad fortune that should normalize.

James Harden deserves credit for remaining a viable offensive engine for as long as he has. Genius passing, scoring craft, a trailblazing exploitation of the gather step and plenty of experience against top defenders allowed him to maintain a relatively high level deep into his 30s.

What was once a gentle decline has now gone over a cliff.

Harden, who inked a fully guaranteed three-year, $96.5 million contract over the offseason, has been overtaken by Father Time.

On pace to post his lowest scoring and assist averages since his first season with the Rockets in 2012-13, Harden is struggling mightily to create separation or score inside the arc. He's not getting past defenders and can't finish near the basket, which is producing an array of off-balance, low-efficiency shot attempts. His 50.0% effective field-goal percentage, driven down by a 39.7 percent conversion rate on two-pointers, is one of the worst of his career.

It certainly doesn't help that the NBA is cracking down on foul-baiting by offensive players, something that was once among Harden's superpowers. This is mostly about natural decline, as it significantly lowers the Cavs' ceiling.

Harden's 32-point outburst on Nov. 11 against the Knicks offered faint hope, but it was an outlier in an otherwise dismal start.

Cooper Flagg is playing like he plans to join LeBron James, Kobe Bryant and Luka Dončić on an extremely short list of 20-year-olds to earn an All-NBA nod.

Flagg's offensive game is hitting a new level in his second season. Kyrie Irving's playmaking is helpful as a pressure release, but this is mostly about clear growth from the reigning Rookie of the Year.

Now, toting a pull-up mid-range that is effectively automatic, Flagg is also getting to the foul line 6.7 times per game while handing out an average of 6.5 assists. Both are well above last year's rates. They're coming alongside defensive play that looks much more like what was described in his prospect profile.

The best (very) young player in the league is demonstrably better than he was during an award-worthy rookie season. Flagg still hasn't ironed out his three-point shot. When he does, he'll be among the most complete two-way forces in the sport. At this rate, he should get there by January.

The sun hasn't set on the Denver Nuggets' days as first-tier contenders, but early returns suggest Nikola Jokić and Co. are entering their twilight phase.

The Nuggets managed a meager 84 points against a healthy Oklahoma City Thunder team in their opener, then suffered home losses to the Warriors and Blazers. The league's top offense last season looks less potent than it has at any point during Jokić's reign. The three-time MVP, while still a brilliant orchestrator, has lost a tick or two off his fastball.

Yes, it's weird to say that about a player who's very likely to average a triple-double. But it's true. Jokić is less mobile and engaged on defense. He's effectively lost his ability to make threes. Even those money-in-the-bank floaters and flip shots are rimming out more often.

As long as Jokić, Jamal Murray and Aaron Gordon are relatively healthy, there's no danger of Denver missing the playoffs. We know what the apex-predator version of this team looks like, as the current iteration just doesn't measure up.

Compared to last year, the Detroit Pistons are shooting the lights out. That's a point in favor of the team's decision to address last season's frequent offensive failures by adding a bunch of gunners to the rotation. While returners Duncan Robinson and Daniss Jenkins are leading the charge by drilling over 40.0 percent of their treys, newcomer John Collins is more than pulling his weight as a floor-stretcher.

Despite a hot shooting start, it still feels like the defensively dominant Pistons have only halfway solved their problems.

The offense still depends heavily on Cunningham (see his 52-point, zero-turnover effort in an overtime win on Nov. 12). Ausar Thompson hasn't shown enough in his expanded on-ball role to suggest Detroit's secondary playmaking has improved at all.

Thompson's presence on the floor knocks the Pistons' offensive rating down by almost 6.0 points per 100 possessions. Their most commonly used lineup without Cunningham scores 103 points per 100 possessions , a low figure.

With a star like Cunningham and a defense this good, Detroit isn't in trouble. But adding shooting still feels like a half-measure.

Not even Yaxel Lendeborg's college head coach knew this was coming. If Dusty May had believed the No. 11 pick had this kind of offensive dominance in him, Lendeborg would have come off the board at No. 9 instead of Michigan teammate Morez Johnson Jr.

May and Dallas' loss is the Warriors' gain, as Lendeborg has given the aging and unathletic Dubs a reason to believe there's hope beyond Stephen Curry.

Lendeborg has racked up multiple 30-point games, physically overpowered opponents on drives, drilled loads of pull-up threes and generally outplayed every rookie in the 2026 class. He's huge and aggressive. He can create his own shot and draw fouls. As a result, Lendeborg very often runs the offense whenever Curry is off the floor.

Lendeborg is in for a true test now, though. After Curry suffered an abdominal injury against the Rockets on Nov. 11, Golden State's season may depend on the rookie's readiness for full-time, first-option work.

Well, it turns out Fred VanVleet was really as important as everyone thought.

While the Houston Rockets still need to worry about Amen Thompson's nonexistent jumper and the inevitable improvement of their opponents' 30th-ranked three-point accuracy , everything just runs more smoothly with the veteran guard back in the fold.

FVV is only averaging 13.7 points per game and may have lost a step after tearing his ACL, but he's a stabilizing presence in the locker room and on the floor. His reintroduction to the lineup puts Thompson into a right-sized offensive role and has allowed Alperen Sengun to access the best version of his game.

Houston will still face postseason problems because defenses won't honor the outside shots of Sengun or Thompson, but this group is a lock to win another 50-plus regular-season games.

A full season is a long time to wait, but Indiana Pacers fans endured the layoff while Tyrese Haliburton got healthy. Their patience has yet to be rewarded.

Haliburton went down with a hamstring strain after just four games, leading a list of several sidelined Pacers in what was supposed to be a redemptive season. There's still time for Indy to get right, recapture the magic of 2024-25, and give its supporters what they've waited for. Alarm bells should remain silent less than a month into the season.

At the same time, it's now harder to imagine the Pacers regaining their peak form.

A key ingredient in the secret sauce of their Finals run was a high-intensity, movement-heavy, fast-paced style that put extreme physical demands on the players. If Haliburton, Ivica Zubac, TJ McConnell and others are already showing signs of breakdown, how can they be expected to hold up when they return?

We don't mean "poised" in the sense of composure, even if the LA Clippers are mostly led by vets who've seen enough to keep their cool in high-leverage moments. We mean it in more of a "ready and waiting" kind of way, as LA will eventually be in position to derive some positive value from a season that is otherwise circling the drain.

With Derrick Jones Jr., Kris Dunn, Brook Lopez and Max Strus, the Clips have a stable of useful and healthy (fingers crossed on that one) veterans who should be in high demand when trade season picks up. Though they're out five first-rounders as punishment for cap circumvention, the Clippers should be able to recoup real assets by shipping out a ton of valuable expiring salaries.

While it might be tempting to see what the team looks like with a healthy Brandon Ingram next to Darius Garland, the wiser course is for the struggling Clippers to stay patient before pouncing on the trade market.

In the wake of a controversial offseason, many agreed the Los Angeles Lakers gave up way too much for Walker Kessler, failed to build a supporting cast with enough reliable three-and-D role players and were generally headed for a disappointing season that might even prompt Luka Dončić to consider playing elsewhere.

Dončić is among the MVP front-runners and definitely the favorite to win a scoring title. Most of Los Angeles' other maligned moves have worked out just fine. Austin Reaves is justifying his new deal by playing like a top option whenever Dončić isn't on the floor. Kessler is captaining a competent defense, as the support pieces are pulling their weight.

It turns out the secondary players tend to fall into place when the primary one, Dončić, plays like he's got everything to prove.

The Memphis Grizzlies have more going for them than an explosive Ty Jerome.

A deep roster that spreads minutes around to an extreme degree ensures the Grizzlies are always fresher and playing harder than their opponents. Steps forward from the likes of Cedric Coward, Jaylen Wells, GG Jackson and Zach Edey all mattered in Memphis' remarkable 7-0 start.

But none of the Grizzlies' surprising success would have happened if Jerome hadn't drilled every wrong-footed, seemingly off-balance floater he tried.

It's not just Jerome's herky-jerky cadence and craft around the basket that has made him the most unexpected star in the league. He's also draining threes, playing with the unbridled confidence of a multi-time All-NBA honoree and thriving in Memphis' unrelenting offensive style.

Tougher times lie ahead as the Grizzlies' scorching three-point shooting inevitably cools, but Jerome and his arsenal of floaters will still let the team levitate on most nights.

Feel is a tricky thing to evaluate, but Doc Rivers doesn't think Giannis Antetokounmpo has any. Opponents who've stood in and "felt" him on his trademarked downhill drives might beg to differ.

While Rivers' controversial comments contained some of his on-brand responsibility evasion, they also might have helped explain the Miami Heat's struggles. Sure, Giannis is bludgeoning defenders and putting up stats as usual, but the Heat haven't quite figured out how to build a sensible system around a player who, in fairness to Rivers, really does just put his head down and go.

Bam Adebayo has yet to figure out where to fit in, Andrew Wiggins looks lost and Klay Thompson's elite shooting isn't making up for his lack of defensive mobility. Though Miami has seen success after its 0-4 start, four of its five wins came against pushovers in the Pacers, Clippers, Kings and Jazz.

Beating good teams will require cohesion and a little more tactical variety. It remains to be seen whether that's possible with Antetokounmpo as the focal point.

The Milwaukee Bucks beat the Pacers by eight on Oct. 26, but have otherwise been suffering blowout loss after blowout loss in their first year of a post-Giannis existence.

Of their first 11 defeats of the season, nine came by double-digit margins. Three of them ended by at least 25 points.

Other than Tyler Herro and Jaime Jaquez Jr., nobody on the roster has managed to score at a decent volume with any level of efficiency. A shockingly immobile Myles Turner has been totally unable to firm up the defensive back line or control the glass.

If you think this is bleak, just wait until a potential punishment for cap circumvention related to Gary Trent Jr.'s offseason contract. If the league docks the Bucks a couple of their distant first-round picks, it's going to be difficult to see any light at the end of the tunnel.

Even LaMelo Ball's staunchest advocates would agree that, for all of his many good qualities, "stability" hasn't exactly been baked into the profile. To be clear, Ball's tendency toward wild on-court decisions and general joie de vivre are net positives; they're part of the reason he's been such an electrifying offensive force when healthy.

It's pretty shocking that a player basically defined by his wild-card nature has helped keep the Minnesota Timberwolves consistent and functional after losing Anthony Edwards to injury.

Minnesota is on pace to best last year's 49 wins and is thriving to the tune of a plus-15.9 net rating swing when Ball is on the court. For his part, the swashbuckling point guard is hitting 40.6 percent of his 8.8 three-point attempts per game while finishing at career-best rates inside the arc. Remarkably, Minnesota has also resisted the urge to overextend the injury-prone Ball, limiting him to what would be a career-low 27.5 minutes per game.

That Ball is averaging a career-worst 4.0 turnovers per contest almost feels reassuring. At least there's still a little wildness in him.

It's great when a single word can describe a team's start in more than one way. We've got one such instance here.

First, second-year big man Derik Queen needed to take a couple of laps around the floor of a live game that his team was losing by 50 points. His frustration is relatable; the New Orleans Pelicans are prone to stretches of listless play that necessitate a little cool-down walk. You try keeping a level head when you're getting blown out to such an extreme degree.

Second, the Pelicans under new head coach Jamahl Mosley have been lapped by the field tactically. Never known for offensive innovation with the Magic, Mosley has the Pels sitting dead last in three-point attempt rate—a long way behind No. 29. While substandard shooting personnel partly explains the issue, there's really no excuse for taking fewer than 30.0 percent of your shots from beyond the arc in 2026.

The three-point revolution is a decade old. Somebody should tell the Pels to get with the times.

The New York Knicks are paying Karl-Anthony Towns $57 million in what will almost certainly be the final year of his contract. Even in NBA terms, that's a lot of money.

Towns owns a $61 million player option for next season that he'll surely decline if he doesn't get an extension, something the Knicks weren't prepared to give him over the offseason. Instead of sulking or mailing it in after helping the Knicks to their first title in a half-century, Towns went to work.

On track to lead the league in rebounding, playing as focused defensively as he ever has and posting the highest effective field-goal percentage of a career defined by shooting efficiency, KAT is playing perhaps his best ball ever.

In doing so, he's taken full possession of the negotiating high ground and further endeared himself to Knicks fans. Towns has done everything asked of him in circumstances where many players would pout or agitate for an exit. For that, owner James Dolan and the Knicks are deeply indebted to him.

When you lose three starters to major injuries in the same game, it's hard to accept the idea that mere bad luck is to blame. Whether you're inclined to buy black magic or some kind of "Weapons"-esque voodoo as the explanation, you've got to concede that something otherworldly befell the Oklahoma City Thunder early this year.

Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace are both likely lost for the season, while Chet Holmgren has an 8-to-10-week timeline for his comparatively minor patellar tendon tear. Losing three players of that caliber would be devastating in any circumstance, but it stings even more for an OKC team that sent out three rotation mainstays—Aaron Wiggins, Lu Dort and Isaiah Joe—to cut costs over the summer.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander still has help in the form of Isaiah Hartenstein, Ajay Mitchell, Jaylin Williams, Jared McCain, Alex Caruso and rookie Aday Mara. That group fought through adversity to start 8-4. All things considered, that's a remarkably good result.

Multiple members of the starting five have already missed significant time. That has made points hard to come by. In other words, these are the Orlando Magic we've come to know and love over the last several years.

Paolo Banchero went down early. Jalen Suggs got injured soon after, limiting the upside of a squad that showed some initial signs of positive change. During their first couple of games, the Magic got stellar play from Banchero and some welcome quick-trigger three-point shooting from Desmond Bane and Tristan da Silva.

While Orlando has continued to fire away from deep, ranking in the top 10 in three-point attempt frequency for the first time since Stan Van Gundy was in charge more than a decade ago, the team's refreshing offensive philosophy hasn't mattered. Due largely to injuries, Orlando is once again hovering around the bottom of the league in offensive efficiency.

That story is all too familiar to Magic fans.

Clutch Player of the Year is basically a crapshoot award every season. Few stats have less year-over-year predictive value than a team's record in close-and-late situations.

But you have to hand it to the Philadelphia 76ers: So far, they've been the league's best clutch team.

Philly is a remarkable 8-0 with a plus-40.8 net rating in games where the score is within five points in the last five minutes. It's up to you to decide whether that's a sign the Sixers have been squeaking by on a thin margin and are therefore overrated, or whether they're proving their ability to win the tight games they hope to experience in the playoffs.

The best teams tend to avoid clutch situations altogether by blowing out their opponents. Philadelphia certainly isn't doing that. Does it still count for something that a roster filled with new players is pulling out close wins without fully developed chemistry? Are the Sixers actually way worse than their record suggests?

Miles Bridges hasn't played anywhere near well enough to justify the price (an unprotected 2033 first-round pick) the Phoenix Suns paid to get him. Jalen Green is showing no signs of rehabilitating his trade value. A roster oddly built without a point guard is—shocker!—often having a hard time scoring.

Phoenix's offensive rating with Bridges, Green, Devin Booker and Dillon Brooks on the floor together ranks in the seventh percentile.

The Suns deserve credit for four of their last five, but the overall picture is bleak. Bad deals populate the books, draft capital is basically nonexistent and Khaman Maluach, one of the few potentially inspiring young players in the mix, has looked unready for real minutes.

Phoenix surprised everyone by winning 45 games a year ago, but that figure could represent a high-water mark for the next decade or so.

Coming into 2026-27, Deni Avdija seemed destined for an ill-advised role reduction. After breaking out as a first-option offensive weapon last year, the Portland Trail Blazers' rising star figured to lose on-ball chances to new addition Ja Morant and returning icon Damian Lillard.

Instead, an injury bumped Morant from the rotation, while Lillard quietly accepted a bit of a backseat. Perhaps most importantly, the Blazers realized it would be absurd to minimize their best player.

After leading the league in drives per game last year, Avdija is as hard-charging as ever. He ranks a solid second in that stat this season. Nobody averages more assists per game on drives or gets to the foul line more often when attacking downhill.

Thankfully, Portland understood how impactful Avdija became last year and figured out how to add talent around him without taking away his touches. The reward could be the 26-year-old's first career All-NBA nod.

The Sacramento Kings haven't lit the beam often this season. That's disappointing because it's genuinely one of the league's better celebratory gimmicks. For that matter, it's been tough to see much light in an otherwise dark, gloomy campaign.

Look harder to see a tiny ray of hope shining through in the shape of rookie Darius Acuff Jr.

Efficiency is going to escape him all season because Acuff is tasked with a preposterously large role and subsists on a diet of tough shots. But if you're not seeing real lead-guard potential in the 20-year-old, you're not paying attention.

Lightning quick, bold, clever with the ball and nowhere near his peak as a foul-baiting grifter, Acuff is atop the league in minutes per game and running away with the team scoring lead at 26.4 points per game. If he holds onto that figure, it'll be the highest rookie scoring average since Michael Jordan put up 28.2 points in 1986.

The San Antonio Spurs have no reason to be alarmed. It's everyone else that should be freaking out.

Experimenting with an odd three-guard lineup hasn't caused any real issues after a 0-2 start. Through San Antonio's first dozen games, its preferred starting group, which features Dylan Harper alongside De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle, Devin Vassell and galaxy-devouring center Victor Wembanyama, owns a plus-27.9 net rating .

That's a wild number for a team that's still clearly working out the kinks tactically.

The Spurs are getting 40- and 50-point games from Wemby, despite still not totally understanding how best to utilize him offensively. Teams aren't guarding Stephon Castle above the arc. Free-agent signee Tobias Harris hasn't even played yet. Other contenders are showing cracks or losing swaths of their rosters to injury.

It's scary out here for everyone hoping to knock off the Spurs.

It's no surprise that Kawhi Leonard (or Immanuel Quickley, for that matter) has faced early-season availability issues. History says missed time was priced in for both.

That didn't make it any easier to watch Scottie Barnes struggle in a first-option role, which many hoped he could handle after last postseason's promising showing. The point of adding Leonard was that Barnes could slot into a more secondary playmaking role but still elevate his game when needed.

Barnes has had his moments, like when he racked up 41 points in a loss to Orlando. Limited to just eight games by an adductor strain, he's had a hard time scoring efficiently and limiting his turnovers. Barnes is shooting well below 20.0 percent from three and is on track to blow past his career-high 2.8 giveaways per game.

Don't give up on the Raptors, who should slot everyone back into their properly sized roles when healthy. You may want to consider Barnes a bit overextended as a primary scoring option.

The Utah Jazz's top two minutes leaders are 19 and 20 years old, respectively. Any team depending so heavily on Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey is naturally going to look a little unready.

In another sense, the Jazz have seemed blindsided by their first foray into actual competitive basketball. For the last several years, Utah hoarded draft assets and losses, often deliberately manipulating lineups and rest nights to ensure a better lottery position.

Maybe a return to honest competition isn't as easy as flipping a switch. That's why the Jazz lost 11 of their first 12 games while failing to deliver on their offensive promise.

It doesn't help that the vision of this team changed abruptly when Walker Kessler was traded to the Lakers and Jaren Jackson Jr. went down early with an injury. But it's hard to avoid the feeling that the Jazz just weren't conditioned to play at the level of the rest of the league.

AJ Dybantsa doesn't yet have the numbers to validate his No. 1 draft position, but the suddenness of his attack to the basket and his ideal big-wing frame matter more when projecting how great he might become.

The interesting thing with the Washington Wizards so far is that they might have more than one foundational young player in the fold. Kyshawn George is older than Dybantsa at 23, but his continued development into a two-way, do-it-all wing should have Wizards fans ecstatic about the future.

George already has six 20-point games after logging 10 all of last year (during a far less competitive Wizards season). His development as an on-ball creator has him on track to set a new career high with 4.8 assists per game. Pair that with intense perimeter defense and startling shot-blocking for a wing, and the third-year pro is well on his way to some Most Improved votes.

Washington is still mostly defined by its imported vets, but if Anthony Davis winds up getting traded and/or Trae Young continues to misfire from deep, a pair of younger up-and-comers could form a new foundation.

Stats courtesy of NBA.com , Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass . Salary info via Spotrac .

Grant Hughes covers the NBA for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, where he appears with Bleacher Report's Dan Favale .

articles.title: Blockbuster NBA Trade Idea To Shake Up the Eastern Conference
articles.summary: The Orlando Magic have so far resisted breaking up the duo of Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner. Conventional wisdom suggests they'll give in soon enough.
articles.body:
The Orlando Magic have so far resisted breaking up the duo of Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner. Conventional wisdom suggests they'll give in soon enough.

Already close to the second apron , the Magic are only going to get more expensive from here. That wouldn't be a problem if they were perched atop the standings and contending for a title. But they're not.

Up until now, playing the "injury" and "head coach" cards helped stave off the most nuclear options. Those justifications no longer hold as much weight. Orlando has changed the head coach, and at some point, also must accept injuries are part of this core's DNA.

Fortunately, there is a trade that would lighten the Magic's long-term cap sheet without nuking their chances at making a ruckus in the Eastern Conference.

Brooklyn Nets Receive: Franz Wagner, Goga Bitadze, Jonathan Isaac

Orlando Magic Receive: Michael Porter Jr., Day'Ron Sharpe, Philadelphia's 2028 first-round pick (top-eight protection), New York's 2029 first-round pick

Moving Franz Wagner is not so much a vote of no-confidence in him as an attempt to optimize the roster and payroll.

Orlando is speeding toward a financial reckoning after this season. It is within striking distance of the second apron now. With Anthony Black and Tristan Da Silva heading for restricted free agency, it will have to choose between getting more expensive or shallower over the summer.

Bringing in MPJ and Sharpe increases the chances of avoiding too much collateral damage. Porter's contract is up after this season, and he shouldn't cost as much per year to retain as Wagner. Sharpe has a $10 million team option. The Magic can decline it and take the tax savings or consider their center rotation set between him and Wendell Carter Jr.

This may not prevent Orlando from losing one or both of Black and Da Silva, or from looking at Jalen Suggs trades. But this package increases the likelihood they can keep one of Black and TDS, without having to worry about finding a backup 5, while still having a high-end starting wing on the docket.

Losing Wagner's downhill attacking, passing and defensive malleability comes as a blow. The Magic have to get past it. MPJ upgrades the spacing as one of the game's most dangerous off-ball and transition spacers. Though he won't replicate Wagner's playmaking and self-creation, he has shown that he can generate more of his own looks since joining Brooklyn.

Others would prefer Orlando to move Paolo Banchero over Wagner if they're forced to choose. On-off data supports that logic. But Franz's solo minutes have been shakier this season . The three-point shot remains a huge limitation the Magic don't have the personnel to overcome. They have also proven more likely to play through Banchero come postseason time.

Getting two first-rounders is a huge help, too. Pushing them past this year is even smarter. This year's draft class isn't receiving much praise, and the Magic don't have their own first in 2028. That 2029 Knicks pick has real upside when you look at the age of their core and James Dolan's asinine refusal to enter the second apron .

Because they have Franz Wagner's brother. Duh.

Oh, also, Brooklyn still needs a primary cornerstone. Egor Dëmin optimists ( *raises hand* ) know it isn't him. Maybe it's Mikel Brown Jr., but it'll be a few years before he has the body and playmaking chops to run the offense. The latter development isn't guaranteed, either.

Wagner comes in and fills this void, if not permanently, then at least in the interim. His shooting limitations aren't ideal, but both of the Nets' backcourt pillars are viable outside shooters. The dynamic between these three should be peachy keen.

Shaky surrounding talent in mind, Brooklyn is probably better equipped to boost spacing around Wagner's interior assaults. At the very least, the Nets will have the assets and spending power to add better complements.

This trade eats up a huge chunk of Brooklyn's cap space, but the Nets still have avenues to league-best(ish) room. While Wagner's fit with Julius Randle isn't awesome, it's only temporary. Randle has just one year left on his deal (player option).

The cost paid here is not insubstantial. It's also not unreasonable. The Nets aren't giving up any of their own future picks or a core player. General manager Sean Marks will need to scour the ranks for a big-picture center with or without Sharpe.

Landing Wagner does not complete Brooklyn's rebuild. But it gives the franchise a clearer path forward.

Dan Favale is a National NBA Writer for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky ( @danfavale ), and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, co-hosted by Bleacher Report's Grant Hughes .

articles.title: NBA Cup 2026 Standings, Bracket Predictions After Group Play on Nov. 13
articles.summary: A handful of upsets in Friday's NBA Cup games altered expectations in certain groups.
articles.body:
A handful of upsets in Friday's NBA Cup games altered expectations in certain groups.

The New York Knicks fell to the Indiana Pacers in East Group B, a loss that put them at 0-2 with two games to play.

The Chicago Bulls got past the Atlanta Hawks in overtime without their rookie phenom Caleb Wilson. That results shook up the complexion of East Group C, which belongs to the Boston Celtics even more than it did before Friday.

Perhaps the most stunning result of all came from the Los Angeles Clippers, who knocked off the Oklahoma City Thunder at home.

OKC isn't out of the running for first place in West Group B yet, but their chances dropped a bit with Friday's surprise loss.

The Knicks dropping to 0-2 in East Group B was not expected by anyone.

Jalen Brunson and Co. aren't mathematically eliminated from reaching the knockout round yet, but they'll need to beat the Miami Heat and Cleveland Cavaliers and then receive some help to advance.

Both of the Knicks' remaining group-stage games are at home, so there is a chance they try to fight their way back into the knockout-round conversation.

The Philadelphia 76ers were the biggest beneficiary in East Group B on Friday night because now they have a path to winning the group by way of wins over Miami and Indiana and a bit of help.

The Sixers lost to the Cavaliers and beat the Knicks in their first two group-stage games. They'd need Cleveland to lose one more time, which is possible against New York, to avoid losing the group on a head-to-head tiebreaker.

The path is clear in East Groups A and C for the Orlando Magic and Boston Celtics to cruise into the knockout round.

Boston's biggest threat appeared to be the Atlanta Hawks, but they fell to the Caleb Wilson-less Chicago Bulls on Friday.

The Celtics get the Hawks at home on November 27 to close out group play. Three days prior, they visit the Washington Wizards. Jayson Tatum and Co. are expected to win both games.

Orlando gets the Detroit Pistons at home on November 24 in the game that will likely decide East Group A.

Detroit is off to an 8-3 start, but the game in Orlando comes at the end of a swing in which the Pistons play five of six on the road. That could play a factor in the November 24 meeting.

Detroit and whichever team finishes second from East Group B will likely battle for the best second-place spot. The Pistons have the chance to run up the score on the Milwaukee Bucks and Toronto Raptors and secure the better point differential, while most East Group B games are expected to be tight.

The Los Angeles Clippers' surprising home win over the Oklahoma City Thunder changed OKC's outlook a bit in West Group B.

OKC gets the Minnesota Timberwolves at home on November 25 in a game many expect to decide first place in West Group B.

The Thunder have to avoid a loss in that contest because they don't have the buffer to advance as the best second-place team anymore. Advancing with two losses, albeit not impossible, is tough in this group-stage format.

Before Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Co. focus on Minnesota, they have to get rid of their current three-game losing streak that also featured back-to-back defeats to the Portland Trail Blazers.

Minnesota's only road trip in the next two weeks is to OKC. The run of home games should allow the Wolves to rest up and build up even more momentum than they already have for the clash in Oklahoma.

West Group A feels like a three-team race between the Dallas Mavericks, Denver Nuggets and Houston Rockets.

Houston visits Denver on Friday for a game it has to win since it already lost to Dallas.

The Nuggets received the luck of the scheduling draw to get the Mavericks and Rockets at home. That could end up being the difference in a tight group.

The San Antonio Spurs are probably going to run away with West Group C. They've already proved they could win big in Portland, which they have to do again in group-stage play on November 25 and then they need to beat the Los Angeles Lakers two days later at home.

If the Blazers and Lakers lose to the Spurs, the best second-place finisher will be down to the West Group A runner-up and Minnesota, if it loses to OKC.

articles.title: Pistons Must Convince Mavs to Make Kyrie Irving Trade for Landscape-Altering Move amid NBA Rumors<br
articles.summary: The Detroit Pistons have found a winning formula with MVP-level play from Cade Cunningham and an elite defense.
articles.body:
The Detroit Pistons have found a winning formula with MVP-level play from Cade Cunningham and an elite defense.

They've also seen the limitations of this design.

They are, without a doubt, one of the NBA's top teams. Yet, it's hard to place them within the inner circle of championship contenders when the same issue that tripped them up last postseason—the lack of a second creator and scorer alongside Cunningham—has yet to be addressed.

If the Pistons could lab-create this co-star for Cunningham, they might build something bearing a striking resemblance to Kyrie Irving: historically shifty off the dribble, wildly efficient as a scorer and even championship-experienced in this very role. An Irving trade feels like a no-brainer for Detroit, then, if it can just convince the Dallas Mavericks to play ball.

That reportedly won't be easy. Not yet, anyway. Between Dallas' hot start and the smooth-as-silk on-court connection between Irving and Cooper Flagg, this situation has The Athletic's Sam Amick ready to declare "I'd lean strongly toward Irving staying put at this point."

And yet, front-office folks haven't ditched the idea of an Irving deal.

"When you talk to rival teams about players who would truly change the playoff landscape if they were dealt, and who are widely expected to generate serious interest because of that belief, Irving still tops the list," Amick wrote. "Never mind that the Mavericks, and Irving for that matter, have shown no signs of wanting a split. Quite the opposite, in fact."

Is this all just wishful thinking from NBA organizations not based in Dallas? Perhaps, but even if it's nothing more, it still stems from a place of logical thought.

The Mavericks have a 19-year-old centerpiece in Flagg. They have very little in the way of guaranteed building blocks around him. And since they were previously sacrificing long-term assets to make some win-now attempts with Luka Dončić, they won't have control of their own first-round pick until 2031.

They need a way to brighten their future. And for all the tricks up the sleeve of a magician like Irving, he remains powerless on this particular front.

Irving is 34 years old. He'll turn 35 before the curtains fall on this campaign. He is slated to reach free agency by 2028 at the latest, and he could expedite his visit to next summer by declining a $42.4 million player option for 2027-28.

Are the Mavericks fully willing to ignore all of that for whatever win-now hopes they've generated over the first few weeks? That seems awfully risky, particularly when a team like the Pistons could (and almost certainly would) outfit them with a healthy package of roster-building assets to tailor their team around Flagg's talents—and timeline.

Several teams would probably pay a premium for Irving, in fact, but Detroit has the most credible case for being one Irving acquisition away from making a title run. Cunningham is that good, and so is this defense. The Pistons' trade offer (likely built around Ron Holland II, maybe rookie Ebuka Okorie and draft compensation) would reflect that belief.

This only matters, of course, if the Mavericks are willing to entertain Irving trade talks.

There are reasons to believe they should be, but it falls on the Pistons to communicate those reasons effectively. Because if Detroit finds a way to land Irving, then it may find a way to transform this regular-season success into a midsummer celebration.

articles.title: El Real Madrid reabre el parque de atracciones: el equipo más divertido de Europa
articles.standfirst: Los blancos destrozan rivales y defensas con un juego vertiginoso que encandila a la afición, anotaciones salvajes y actuaciones corales
articles.summary: Los blancos destrozan rivales y defensas con un juego vertiginoso que encandila a la afición, anotaciones salvajes y actuaciones corales
articles.body: Un parque de atracciones ha vuelto a instalarse en Goya, concretamente, en el Movistar Arena. Los encuentros del Real Madrid forman parte de nuevo de la gran oferta de ocio de la ciudad. Ir a verlos es sinónimo de diversión gracias a un juego sensacional, un ritmo trepidante y unas anotaciones salvajes que acostumbran a irse por encima de los 100 puntos. Así es el baloncesto de Pedro Martínez, que tiene encandilada a la afición. Hacía tiempo que la grada del Palacio no disfrutaba tanto con su equipo. Incluso en una derrota, como ante el Panathinaikos en la prórroga tirando de orgullo ante las lesiones. Quizás no se veía nada igual desde la época del 'Lasismo'. Después, salvo en el ejercicio anterior, siguieron cayendo los títulos, pero el juego no fue tan hipnotizador como el actual. El partido de este jueves ante el Estrella Roja, que llegaba como la mejor defensa de la Euroliga, bien podría ser la cumbre de la temporada: 38 puntos en el primer cuarto; 74, los que los serbios encajaban de media, cuando aún restaban 13 minutos; y 105 al final. "El Madrid te mete 100 puntos sin querer", decía en la previa Ibon Navarro, técnico de los serbios. Así es. De los 20 partidos oficiales que han disputado los blancos, en nueve de ellos han llegado a la centena. La temporada pasada alcanzaron esa cifra en 16 de los 84 encuentros. Su media anotadora en la Euroliga es la mejor de la competición: 98,5. Son 10,4 puntos más que el año pasado. En la Liga Endesa, donde marcha invicto y está registrando cifras históricas, se dispara hasta los 106,3 por los 93,8 del curso anterior. El ritmo es la clave de tanto vértigo y para poder marcarlo es fundamental el rebote. El conjunto blanco ha ganado esa batalla en 16 de sus 20 partidos. Si lo atrapa en su aro, a volar. El ofensivo lo carga con fuerza tanto para buscar nuevos tiros como para dificultar la salida del rival. El Madrid es uno de los equipos que juega a más posesiones por partido tanto en la Euroliga como en la ACB. Muchas de ellas las finaliza en el primer tercio, antes de los ocho segundos, aprovechando que la defensa aún no está organizada. El rival casi no ha tirado y ya debe estar pensando en volver atrás. Puede ser un contraataque, un tiro de cualquiera que encuentre buena posición o, por supuesto, un triple. Porque el tiro exterior es uno de los aspectos que más está explotando el Madrid. Desde el inicio de la temporada, Pedro Martínez ya dijo que quería que sus jugadores tiraran más de fuera. Tanto en Euroliga como en Liga son los segundos que más lo intentan: 31,3 sólo por detrás del París Basketball en la primera y 34,6 tras el UCAM Murcia en la segunda. Hace un año lanzaban 26,6 y 27,3, respectivamente. La filosofía es volumen por encima de acierto, aunque este también es extraordinario. Ahí quedan los récords batidos tanto en Euroliga como en ACB en tan sólo cuatro días: 21 al Maccabi Tel Aviv y 20 al Surne Bilbao Basket. En el global de la temporada, los blancos están anotando el 40,4% de los triples que lanzan. Extraordinario porcentaje para una muestra tan elevada. El Madrid se está caracterizando por un juego coral que ya puso en práctica Pedro Martínez en su exitoso paso por el Valencia Basket. Compartir mucho el balón, con 21,8 asistencias de media en lo que va de temporada, y rotaciones constantes para mantener un ritmo alto. Nadie supera los 25 minutos en pista en ninguna de las dos competiciones, en todos los encuentros han anotado un mínimo de 10 jugadores y ya ha habido ocho máximos anotadores distintos en un encuentro. Y todo ello, superando la plaga de lesiones que ha castigado al equipo últimamente. A Usman Garuba, que se perderá toda la temporada o casi, se han sumado Gabriel Deck y Mikael Jantunen también con dolencias de larga duración. Theo Maledon, a nivel de MVP de la Euroliga, y Facundo Campazzo aún siguen de baja. Y Nick Smith Jr. y Chuma Okeke se han perdido citas recientes. "No deberíamos sacar pecho, somos el Madrid. Un buen equipo y buenos jugadores. Es una plantilla larga para solventar esta situaciones", decía Pedro Martínez tras la última victoria. Ni así deja de acelerar el Madrid, que aprovecha las ausencias para dar confianza a quienes lo necesitan: a un Timothé Luwawu-Cabarrot que va a rachas, a un Gabriele Procida que la campaña anterior apenas contó, a un Olivier Sarr que va empezando a encajar, a un Smith al que le está costando el aterrizaje en Europa... Sólo Max Shulga falta por arrancar, aunque ya ha tenido chispazos. Otros efectivos, como Alberto Abalde y Andrés Feliz han elevado su nivel hasta estar en máximos de sus respectivas etapas en el conjunto blanco. La suma de todo ello hace que el Madrid sea uno de los equipos más divertidos de ver en Europa, pero ese juego espectacular tendrá que traducirlo en títulos. El primero en liza, la Supercup de la Euroliga, ya lo conquistó. En febrero llega la Copa del Rey y después, en mayo y junio, los dos premios gordos. Queda mucho, pero el camino, por ahora, está siendo disfrutón.

articles.title: Ziaire Williams On JJ Redick’s ‘Audit’ Of Lakers’ 11-2 Record: “You Would Think We Almost Last”
articles.summary: JJ Redick audited the Lakers' season thus far on Friday, and Ziaire Williams loved it.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Lakers are tied for the best record in the NBA at 11-2, but head coach JJ Redick isn't satisfied with what he has seen from his team. Redick shared at practice on Friday that the Lakers had spent time earlier in the day auditing their start to the 2026-27 season.

"Just wanted to take today as more of an audit," Redick said, via Infanity TV. "We gave our analytics guys a bunch of stuff that we had questions about. We reviewed that for about an hour and a half this morning in our coaches' meeting. Had a presentation with the players. What we're doing well, where we need to be better, spend some time on the court walking through stuff."

The Lakers getting three days off between games meant this was the right time to review. Despite having this impressive record, Redick revealed the players were very receptive to the negative feedback. The 42-year-old was then unsurprisingly asked what exactly this process was like.

"We talked a little bit on the road trip, talked a lot yesterday," Redick said. "I had about 20 things. Greg [St. Jean] and Ty [Abbott] and Nate [McMillan] had about 20 things on the defensive end. Our analytics guys put together a 21-page presentation that we went over this morning, and we filtered through our offensive stuff based on our identities of who we want to be offensively: organized, unselfish, advantage-based."

"Then we went through the stats on that, and then we went to our defense," Redick continued. "And our three identities: organized, physical as f***, and relentless. And we went through the stats based on those things. And so it's a very clean thing. We've done that for the last two and a half seasons. It's just everything that we present to the team lines up with who we're trying to be."

The Lakers' 121.6 offensive rating is the best in the NBA, while their 113.6 defensive rating ranks 18th. You'd imagine there were far more negatives pointed out regarding the defense than the offense. Lakers forward Ziaire Williams was asked about this audit at practice , and it appears the coaching staff didn't hold back.

"It was good," Williams said, via Infanity TV. "A lot of good things and a lot of things to clean up. Being first in the West with the stuff that they showed us, you would think we almost last… Got to keep us honest. But it's good to know that there's still room for growth, as good as we're doing. So yeah, it was great. Hopefully we'll clean that up on next game against Phoenix."

Redick and his staff wouldn't want these players to get carried away. They have deservedly been showered with praise with this hot start, but need to keep up the good work.

While Luka Doncic , Austin Reaves , and Walker Kessler have dominated headlines, Williams has done pretty well, too. The 25-year-old is averaging 11.0 points, 2.6 rebounds, 2.0 assists, 1.5 steals, and 0.2 blocks per game in 2026-27. He has been ridiculously efficient, shooting 56.3% from the field and 46.5% from beyond the arc.

The Lakers signed Williams to a one-year, $3 million deal, and that's looking like a good piece of business right now. He was primarily brought in for his defense, and has fared better on offense than you'd have expected.

With Reaves suffering a heel injury in Wednesday's 123-111 win over the Milwaukee Bucks , the Lakers might need more offensively from Williams. The star guard isn't expected to miss too much time, though, as Redick revealed he is day-to-day .

Reaves is likely to be missing when the Lakers face the Phoenix Suns next at Mortgage Matchup Center on Sunday at 4 p.m. ET. They'll be looking to make it eight straight wins that night, and you'd fancy their chances against the 5-6 Suns.

articles.title: Wemby Reacts to Draymond Green's Shove with Honest Response in Viral Video After Spurs Beat Warriors
articles.summary: San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama had a matter-of-fact response when asked Friday night about Golden State Warriors forward Draymond Green committing a flagrant foul by pushing him in the back.
articles.body:
San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama had a matter-of-fact response when asked Friday night about Golden State Warriors forward Draymond Green committing a flagrant foul by pushing him in the back.

Speaking to reporters following the Spurs' 123-85 win over the Warriors, Wemby said, "It's not surprising," when asked about the shove:

The play in question occurred during the second quarter with San Antonio leading by 23 points. Green was assessed a flagrant foul 1, and Wembanyama made the ensuing free throw.

Green is no stranger to physical play that often toes and even crosses the line of the rulebook.

He is tied for second in the NBA in technical fouls this season with three, and he has finished in the top 10 in techs every year since the 2017-18 season.

Despite hitting the floor hard on the Green foul, it was a relatively easy night for Wembanyama on Friday.

The 7'4" Frenchman only played 21 minutes due to the Spurs being in control throughout, and he finished with 12 points, 12 rebounds, six assists and two blocks.

Stephon Castle led the way for the Spurs with 32 points, but they largely employed a well-balanced attack between the starters and bench players, as no other player on the team reached 20 points.

As for Green, he managed just four points, three rebounds and three assists in 16n minutes during the one-sided loss.

The Warriors were without superstar guard Stephen Curry, who is expected to miss at least two weeks due to an oblique tear suffered Wednesday.

With Curry on the shelf, Golden State couldn't do much of anything offensively against San Antonio, shooting just 33 percent from the field.

The Warriors have no lost back-to-back games on the heels of an eight-game winning streak, dropping their record to 8-5 on the season.

Meanwhile, the reigning Western Conference champion Spurs look every bit like a title contender, as their 11-2 mark is tied for the best in the West.

If there is any bad blood between the Spurs and Warriors over Green's shove, the two sides won't get a chance to settle it until Jan. 30, which is the next time they are scheduled to play each other.

articles.title: 'I'm F--ked Up,' Yaxel Reacts to Warriors Losing 'By Like 100' to Wemby, Spurs with Curry Injured
articles.summary: Golden State Warriors rookie forward Yaxel Lendeborg was up front about his frustration following a 123-85 loss to the San Antonio Spurs on Friday night.
articles.body:
Golden State Warriors rookie forward Yaxel Lendeborg was up front about his frustration following a 123-85 loss to the San Antonio Spurs on Friday night.

After Golden State's disappointing performance without injured star Stephen Curry, Lendeborg told reporters , "We just lost by like 100. So you know I'm f--ked up mentally right now."

Lendeborg, who finished with just three points on 1-of-13 shooting from the field, added, "I was flustered the entire game. Couldn't make a damn layup."

For the No. 11 overall pick out of Michigan, Friday marked the worst showing of his young NBA career thus far.

Prior to that, Lendeborg was enjoying a Rookie-of-the-Year-caliber season, and he is still very much in the conversation for that award thanks to averages of 20.2 points, 7.4 rebounds and 3.5 assists per game.

The hope and expectation among the Warriors and their fans was that Lendeborg would be able to step up and raise his game to an even higher level while Curry is out of action.

Curry left Wednesday's loss to the Houston Rockets and was later diagnosed with an oblique tear , which is expected to keep him out for at least two weeks.

Lendeborg admitted to reporters that his confidence level in picking up the slack for Curry was a "six out of 10," before adding, "The other four is like, man, am I going to be able to live up to it? Am I going to be able to help out the team the way I want to? But time will tell."

The 24-year-old budding star suggested that the looming presence of Spurs center Victor Wembanyama in the paint altered the way he and his teammates approached things on Friday.

"Nobody wanted to go into the paint," Lendeborg said. "Nobody wanted to get their shot blocked by him. So we were all just doing some weak-ass floaters. I don't know how many of us work on those. Especially me. I shot like seven of them. I never work on floaters since like [junior college]."

The result was an awful shooting performance by Lendeborg and the Warriors as a whole, as they shot just 33 percent from the field as a team.

Golden State also lost its second straight game following an eight-game winning streak, dropping its record to 8-5 on the year.

While that is still a solid mark, there is cause for concern if the way the Warriors played without Curry on Friday becomes a trend rather than an isolated incident.

A softer landing spot may benefit Lendeborg and the Dubs on Monday when they face the 4-9 New Orleans Pelicans on the road in their next game.

articles.title: Giannis Speaks Out on 'Trust' with Bam, Heat After Blowout Win vs. James Harden, Cavs
articles.summary: Miami Heat forward Giannis Antetokounmpo is encouraged by how his on-court dynamic with Bam Adebayo is trending and the improved play by the team as a whole following Friday's 133-121 win over the Cleveland Cavaliers.
articles.body:
Miami Heat forward Giannis Antetokounmpo is encouraged by how his on-court dynamic with Bam Adebayo is trending and the improved play by the team as a whole following Friday's 133-121 win over the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Speaking to reporters after the game, Antetokounmpo praised improved "trust" that he has with Adebayo as they continue to learn each other's style.

"We're making progress in trust. We need to keep doing our work quietly, humbly," Antetokounmpo said. "There's still a lot of work to be done. We're not even close. Still a lot of work to be done."

Antetokounmpo was also very complimentary toward Adebayo for his "aggressive" play against Cleveland.

"Bam played great, aggressive, got to his spots. I did the same," he said. "Every game will look differently. There will be times like tonight where we will overpower other bigs, but we can't force it."

Antetokounmpo and Adebayo both scored 37 points on Friday night, accounting for 57 percent of the Heat's total scoring output. They also combined for 23 rebounds and five assists.

The 37 points for Adebayo were his most in a game since his 83-point outing against the Washington Wizards last season.

Miami's 133 points were its second-most in a game this season. The Heat have also won three straight and four of their last five to reach the .500 mark (6-6) for the first time all season.

They also held Cleveland's backcourt duo of James Harden and Donovan Mitchell to 14-of-35 shooting from the field.

Antetokounmpo is a 10-time All-Star, nine-time All-NBA player, two-time NBA MVP and 2020-21 NBA champion. He spent his first 13 seasons with the Milwaukee Bucks before they traded him to the Heat on July 6.

Even though Antetokounmpo's individual numbers have been strong with his new team, including 28.5 points and 12.3 rebounds per game, it hasn't translated into as many wins as the Heat were hoping for at this point.

It's still very early in the season and Friday was an indication the duo of Antetokounmpo and Adebayo, as well as head coach Erik Spoelstra, are starting to piece things together.

This level of dominance between the two of them was the hope for Miami after bringing in Antetokounmpo. It is also necessary because the Heat gave up a lot of quality depth from their rotation in the trade.

If the victory over the Cavs leads to more positive play between Antetokounmpo and Adebayo, the Heat can put themselves squarely in the mix with the other top teams in the Eastern Conference.

We will find out how far the Heat have come very soon because they will host the Detroit Pistons (8-3) in the second night of a back-to-back on Saturday night.

articles.title: El Breogán se impone al San Pablo Burgos en un recital histórico
articles.standfirst: Rasir Bolton lidera al equipo gallego con 32 puntos y 50 de valoración
articles.summary: Rasir Bolton lidera al equipo gallego con 32 puntos y 50 de valoración
articles.body: La estratosférica actuación del estadounidense Rasir Bolton (32 puntos y 50 créditos de valoración) guió al Río Breogán a una nueva victoria para mantener vivo su sueño de disputar la Copa del Rey, después de vencer a un San Pablo Burgos (119-110) que llegó con vida a falta de tres minutos y medio, cuando encajó un parcial 11-4 que resultó decisivo. El Breogán se sobrepuso a su mal inicio de partido para resolver en los tres primeros minutos del segundo cuarto, con un parcial 16-2, el problema en el que se había metido por su desacierto exterior (3/13 en triples) y, sobre todo, por su escasa intensidad defensiva. El jamaicano Chase Audige lideró a San Pablo Burgos en el primer cuarto. Breogán, sin intensidad, sufría para frenar el ataque del equipo de Porfirio Fisac, que se despegó en el electrónico tras un parcial 4-13 que forzó el tiempo muerto de Luis Casimiro (14-22, min.8). El parón no frenó a Burgos, que siguió anotando con mucha facilidad. Eso le permitió coger una renta de diez puntos (17-27) antes de entrar en el segundo cuarto, cuando llegó la reacción celeste. Liderado por Tevin Breogán y Rasir Bolton, el Breogán empequeñeció a su rival con una notable mejoría defensiva y un juego mucho vertical en ataque. El equipo de Luis Casimiro había recuperado sus señas de identidad, y eso no tardó en reflejarse en el electrónico. El parcial 14-2 de salida obligó a Porfirio Fisac a detener el encuentro porque a su equipo se le había esfumado su ventaja en poco más de tres minutos. Sin su referente ofensivo, el base estadounidense DJ Stewart, baja por una lesión muscular en los isquiotibiales de la pierna izquierda, Burgos se había apagado en ataque. El vendaval ofensivo del Breogán, además, coincidió con el desacierto exterior de su rival, que no descosió para llegar con vida al descanso (47-38), antes de que las defensas desaparecieran del partido (41-42 fue el resultado del tercer cuarto, la máxima anotación acumulada en un cuarto en la historia de la ACB). El último asalto arrancó con un tiro libre para Rasir Bolton por la falta técnica a Fisac (89-80). Burgos, no obstante, estaba mucho más cómodo y se acercó a dos (89-97) antes de Andric oxigenara a los suyos con un triple y Tevin Brown cometiese su cuarta falta personal. Casimiro no escondió su preocupación. Con 92-90 a falta de siete minutos, pidió tiempo muerto y devolvió a pista a Francis Alonso, que no tardó en aparecer con cinco puntos consecutivos (101-94). El intercambio de golpes favoreció a Breogán, que se agarró a Rasir Bolton para seguir jugando con pequeñas ventajas pese a que Porfirio Fisac pidió un último tiempo muerto (110-103, min.37) en busca de una reacción que no llegó. 119.- Río Breogán (19+28+41+31): Tevin Brown (17), Rasir Bolton (32), Peris (3), Andric (11) y Kasibabu (2) -cinco inicial- Mavra (14), Andersson García (7), Francis Alonso (14), Aranitovic (5), Brankovic (12) y Brimah (2). 110.-San Pablo Burgos (27+11+42+30): Chase Audige (22), Joaquín Taboada (7), Dani Díez (13), Sengfelder (8) y Sekou Doumbouya (24) -cinco inicial- Pablo Almazán (2), Balsa Koprivica (7), Retin Obasohan (12), Dusan Radosavjevic (2) y Raúl Lobaco (13). Árbitros: Martín Caballero, Sergio Manuel y Carlos Merino. Incidencias: Encuentro correspondiente a la octava jornada de la Liga Endesa disputado en el Pazo Provincial dos Deportes de Lugo ante 5.303 espectadores. - Mayor anotación conjunta SIN prórrogas desde 1988: 229 puntos - Han pulverizado la mitad más anotadora en era acb: récord histórico de 144 puntos tras el descanso, superando los 133 del Barça-Cajabilbao 1986-87. - Han protagonizado el cuarto más anotador de la historia con 83 puntos (41-42). El récord anterior era de 73. - Río Breogán Iguala su máxima anotación: 119. - Recoletas Salud San Pablo Burgos iguala su máxima anotación: 110. - Rasir Bolton se convierte en el primer jugador en anotar 32 puntos y dar 11 asistencias en un partido, y el segundo en la historia en llegar a 50 de valoración jugando menos de 30 minutos. Es la sexta mejor valoración de un jugador en el Siglo XXI.

articles.title: Sophie Cunningham Drops Honest Quote on Luka Doncic Comparison by Addressing Contract Differences
articles.summary: Sophie Cunningham's offensive workload was recently compared to Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Doncic, but the Indiana Fever guard quickly shut the comparison down.
articles.body:
Sophie Cunningham's offensive workload was recently compared to Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Doncic, but the Indiana Fever guard quickly shut the comparison down.

On her podcast, No Hesitation , NBA trainer Drew Hanlen detailed how Doncic has already taken 221 shots in nine games, while Cunningham took 226 during the entire 2026 WNBA campaign (h/t Yagya Bhargava of Basketball Network).

Cunningham then pointed to their respective contracts.

Watch: F-15 jets flyover before college football game

NFL Rule Changes on Trade Deadline 'Snafus' and Schedule Eyed, New Rumors Reveal

"You're missing a big one. He also makes $50 million a year. I make $700,000 on my WNBA check," Cunningham said. "You should compare me more to Quentin Grimes. You know, we average around, you know, eight to 10 points. I think that's it. My 3-point shooting is actually better than the both of them. And so if we're going to compare, let's compare."

Doncic is the leader of the Lakers' offense and one of the best scorers in the NBA, while Cunningham is more of a role player for the Fever, so the eye-popping discrepancy in their field goal attempts makes sense.

Perhaps a player like Grimes, who comes off the bench for the Lakers, would be a more accurate NBA comparison for Cunningham.
